activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
story:
The birthday party had spilled from the kitchen into the backyard, where someone's uncle was grilling hamburgers fast enough for the kids to consume two each. Hudson was halfway through his second bun when he noticed the corner by the fence. Three boys from another school circled a kid named Theo, who was holding his slice of cake and pretending not to hear them.

"Nice jacket," one of them said. "Did your mom pick it out?" The others laughed. Theo's shoulders climbed toward his ears, and he set the cake down on the grass like he'd lost his appetite for it.

Hudson's first instinct was to barge over and shout, which would make him the adversary of three bigger boys at once. His second instinct was to do nothing, because what could one person even change? He'd stood by before, at school, and the memory sat badly with him. Was there something in between? He watched the boys and noticed a pattern: they worked off each other's laughter. When one of them paused, the teasing sagged, like a fire losing air. Maybe it didn't need a bucket of water. Maybe it just needed someone to break the circle.

He crossed the lawn, picked up Theo's plate, and held it out. "Hey, they're doing the piñata," he said, as if he'd arrived for no other reason. "You're missing it. Sasha's about to take a blindfolded swing at a crowd of innocent people." He kept his voice easy, not defiant, not scared. The boys blinked. The loudest one glanced at the others, waiting for a cue that didn't come, because the circle had a gap in it now.

"Piñata?" Theo said. He took the plate back and stood up straighter. "Whose dumb idea was candy in the yard?" He walked with Hudson, and the three boys drifted off toward the trampoline like a breeze that had changed direction.

Later, sitting on the porch steps with Sasha, Hudson asked the question that had been circling his head all afternoon. "Does that actually work? Stepping in like that? Or did we just get lucky?" Sasha, who had read every pamphlet in the counselor's office out of pure boredom, nodded. "There was a study of school playgrounds in 2001. When a classmate stepped in to stop bullying, the bullying stopped in more than half of the cases." Hudson turned that over, wondering how many times he'd watched teasing end on its own, and whether it had actually ended because someone quietly stepped in and he'd never noticed.

"More than half," he said. "So you don't even have to win. You just have to walk over there." He looked across the yard, where Theo was now telling the three boys, in detail, exactly why their trampoline technique was wrong. Sasha raised her plastic cup. "To the gap in the circle," she said. Hudson tapped his cup against it.

activity: to read a Shakespeare scene and paraphrase the speeches into modern English
story:
Mathis slid the battered copy of A Midsummer Night's Dream across the library table and stared at the page like it had insulted him personally. "Puck, round about, go and watch," he read aloud, then stopped. Ms. Le had said their homework was to paraphrase the scene, to turn each speech into plain modern English, and so far his notebook held exactly one line: "The fairy says something about the earth."

Nimrit dropped into the chair beside him and peered at the page. "You've been on that scene for twenty minutes."

"It's tedious," Mathis said. "Half the words look like typos." He tapped the paper. "And look here. Every so often the script says exit, which is fine, that's obviously the guy leaving. But then it says this other word, exeunt, and it's not even a name. Who is Exeunt? Why does he keep showing up?" He flipped pages, and the word kept appearing, always at the end of the busiest moments, when three or four fairies were crowding the stage.

Nimrit frowned and counted characters on her fingers. "Wait. Look at that part. Puck exits alone, and it says exit. Then Oberon and Titania both leave together, and it says exeunt. Try the crowded one, the scene where all four of them have been arguing." They found it: four speeches in a row, then the word exeunt, and nobody left on stage.

Mathis sat back so fast his chair squeaked. "It's not a person. Exit is Latin for he or she goes out," he said slowly, testing it. "Exeunt is Latin for they go out. It's used when two or more characters leave." He checked it against every scene ending in the book, and it held every single time. "So it's like a stage traffic signal."

"Okay, so now you can actually see who's on stage," Nimrit said. "Can you paraphrase the speeches now?"

Mathis looked at Puck's long speech again. Some of it was still fog, but now he could see the shape of it, who was speaking to whom, who was staying, who was going. He wrote, "The fairy says the earth is so full of vapor from the oceans that clouds form," and crossed out the fog. It wasn't perfect, but it was real English, his English. He turned the page and kept going.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
story:
Hazel slid her draft across the table in Ms. Nair's classroom, where writing club met every Thursday after last bell. Vincenzo read it, frowned, and tapped one line. "This part sounds weird," he said. "'We need to leave now.' Mom said. 'Before the storm hits.'" He read it aloud twice, and both times it came out sounding like three separate people talking.

Hazel looked at the line and felt her stomach knot. She wanted to read her story aloud at the spring showcase, and Ms. Nair had said every story needed a clear climax, the moment everything turned. Hazel's climax was that line, the moment Mom decided to run. If it sounded broken, the whole ending wobbled.

"Try it out loud," Lucca said from the next seat. "Just the quote. Ignore the Mom said part." Hazel tried. "We need to leave now before the storm hits." One breath. One sentence. So the quote was one sentence, even though the tag sat in the middle of it like a rock in a stream. She circled the period after "now" and the capital B on "Before," then erased both. Now she had a comma before the second quotation mark, and "before" started small. The line read smoothly, and when Vincenzo read it aloud this time, it sounded like one person talking through one sentence.

Ms. Nair began to circulate around the room, pausing at each table. When she reached theirs, Hazel held up the draft. "I think when the tag interrupts one spoken sentence, the second part starts lowercase, because the sentence is still going." Ms. Nair read the line and nodded. "Read it at the showcase," she said, and moved on.

Vincenzo, who had spent three weeks insisting he would never share his own story because nobody would believe a talking dog was plausible, looked at Hazel's page for a long moment. "If your line can get fixed that fast," he said, "maybe mine can too." He pulled his notebook out of his bag.

Hazel remembered the first club meeting in September, when she had written nothing at all and had watched Lucca's pencil move for a whole hour, sure she would never have a story worth fixing. Now her climax line sat on the page, punctuated, whole. She flipped to a fresh sheet and wrote the first line of the showcase introduction: "This is a story about a storm."

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
story:
Leah spread her poster across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with salt shakers. Her assignment was to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death, and she had one column filled: her grandmother's church, heaven, and being with God. The other column was blank because Jaden, who came over every Tuesday, practiced Sikhism, and Leah had promised herself she would get the facts right instead of guessing.

"Okay," she said when Jaden arrived and dumped her backpack on a chair, "I'm going to ask you questions and write down exactly what you say. You can check the poster before I hand it in." Jaden, who wanted her name in the credits as "research partner" because she was angling for a spot on the school news team, pulled out an apple and said that was fair.

"So, after death," Leah began. "Rebirth? Karma?"

"Yes and yes," Jaden said, chewing. "We accept rebirth, and karma too."

Leah wrote it down, then stopped. "Wait. So if you do enough good deeds, you climb up until you escape the whole cycle? Like a ladder?"

Jaden shook her head so hard her ponytail whipped around. "No, that's the part everybody gets wrong. My Sunday school teacher made us memorize it. Guru Nanak taught that the body takes birth because of karma, but salvation comes through God's grace."

Leah stared at her. "Then why do good deeds at all?"

"Good question. I petition God every morning, and I try to serve people, but I don't think of it like paying for a ticket." Jaden tapped the blank column. "Write the quote, then write what it means to me, not a fake version."

Leah tested the idea out loud, the way she tested a math answer backward. "So karma explains the body, the being-born part, and grace is separate. Good deeds matter, but they're not the whole answer, because if they were, grace wouldn't be grace. It would be more like a purchase." Jaden pointed the apple core at her. "Exactly. My cousin calls the ladder idea a counterfeit, because it looks like the real teaching but it isn't."

They worked until the poster's second column was full, and Leah realized the comparison had a shape she hadn't planned: her grandmother's faith and Jaden's both said you could not simply earn your way to God. When Ms. Vargas had set the assignment, Leah had groaned, but now the blank column seemed like the best part.

At the climax of the evening, or at least of the poster, Leah uncapped the glitter glue for the title. "Research partner, Jaden Kaur," she printed along the bottom, in her most careful letters.

"Spell Kaur right," Jaden said, leaning over her shoulder, "or I'm eating the rest of your cookies."

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
story:
Natalie slapped her poster flat on the lab table and weighted the corners with rocks from the supply shelf. Across the top she had written, in her best block letters, "Bigger Beaks Win." Lyndon leaned over it and nodded slowly.

"Sounds right," he said. "Big beaks crack big seeds. Big seeds are tougher, so you need the muscle." He tapped the drawing she had made of a fat-beaked finch, then one of a slim-beaked finch labeled "loser."

"That's what I thought too," Natalie said. "That's why I made the poster before doing the reading." She held up a photocopied article Mr. Rivera had left on the back counter, its margins already crowded with her pencil notes. "But listen to this. On an island called Daphne Major, the medium ground finches got studied for years. Then came the very wet El Niño year, 1983. All that rain brought tons of small, soft seeds."

"So?" Lyndon said.

"So the big beaks stopped winning. Selection went the other way. After 1983 it favoured smaller beaks." She flipped to her drawing and crossed out the word "loser" so hard the pencil tore a little.

Ariella wandered over from the window, where she had been copying the week's homework equation into her planner. "Wait, smaller is better sometimes? That messes up my whole poster too. Mine says the finches that colonize the islands evolved bigger beaks because the hard seeds chose them." She frowned. "Sort of. I'm redoing the arrows."

Natalie remembered the first day of the unit, when Mr. Rivera had set out three trays of seeds on the counter and a box of tweezers, pliers, and spoons. "Pick up your food," he had said, and the class had giggled. Natalie had grabbed the pliers first, certain they were the prize tool, the best beak. Then he had dumped a tray of tiny soft seeds in front of her and she had fumbled with the pliers while Ariella, armed with a spoon, cleaned the tray in seconds. Best tool, she had realized, depends on the food.

"Let's test it," Natalie said now. She fetched the trays from the cabinet. She gave Lyndon the pliers, kept the tweezers for herself, and spread the small soft seeds across the table. "Small seeds. Go." Lyndon clanked the pliers after one seed while she snapped up six. Ariella counted them out loud.

"Six to one," Ariella announced. "Small beak wins."

Natalie uncapped a marker and wrote across her poster, over the old title, "It Depends on the Seeds." Then, underneath, she drew two arrows pointing in opposite directions.

Mr. Rivera paused behind them on his way to the volcano poster, the one with the molten rock flowing down its slopes. He looked at the crossed-out word, the seeds, the tweezers.

"Flip your poster over," he said. "Start there. That one's worth an A."

Natalie flipped it and began to draw.

activity: going to a first school dance
story:
Jasleen's bedroom smelled like hair spray and mint gum, and the dance was in one hour, which meant disaster was imminent if Alexandra could not find her other earring. "It rolled somewhere," Jasleen said, kneeling to look under the bed. Alexandra thought harder than she looked. She had put the earrings on Jasleen's desk, and the desk tilted slightly toward the window, she had noticed that when she set her juice glass down and it slid an inch. So the earring had rolled left, toward the wall. She checked behind the desk's left leg, and there it was, glinting in the lamplight.

"You're like a detective," Jasleen said, clapping. "You figured out where it went without even seeing it move." Alexandra grinned and clipped the earring on. It reminded her of last summer, when her tent had kept collapsing at the lake. Everyone else had just re-staked it over and over, but she had lain on her stomach watching the poles until she saw that one joint was bent, so the whole frame twisted every time the wind came. She had splinted the joint with a stick and tape, and the tent had stood for three more nights. Things usually made sense if you watched long enough.

At the dance, the gym was loud and glittering. Alexandra stood near the wall with her cup of punch while Jasleen went to find Tenzin. Hundreds of small spots of light swept across the floor, the ceiling, the banners, then swung back again. She looked for the source. There was only one spotlight, up on the stage, shining upward at a ball hanging from the rafters. One beam went in, and hundreds of spots came out. She tracked a single spot as it crawled along the bleachers and vanished, and she noticed the ball itself was turning, slowly, and every tiny mirror tile on it caught the beam and threw it somewhere slightly different, like hundreds of tiny doors each opening a different way.

"Are you going to dance or just stare at the ceiling?" Tenzin asked, appearing beside her with Jasleen. "I'm staring at the ceiling, and it's working," Alexandra said, and pointed. "That ball up there is why the whole gym sparkles. One spotlight hits it, and each little mirror tile reflects the beam in a slightly different direction, so we get all these moving spots." Tenzin squinted up. "So there's only one real light?" "One real light, hundreds of reflections," Alexandra said. Jasleen gasped like this was the best news she had ever heard.

Jasleen grabbed Alexandra's hand and pulled her toward the middle of the floor, right into the path of the sweeping spots. "Then we're dancing inside the spotlight, all of it," Jasleen said. Tenzin jogged after them, and the three of them spun slowly under the turning ball, glitter washing over their shoes. "Okay," Alexandra said, laughing as a spot of light landed square on her one found earring. "Now I'm staring at the ceiling and dancing."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Jasmine crouched at the edge of the tide line, holding a piece of sea glass the color of a thermostat's little green screen. The family had driven four hours to the shore, and she had promised herself she would bring something home. Her father had already set up the umbrella. Her little brother, eight and loud, was digging a hole big enough to sit in.

"Look at this," she said when Kayla wandered over from the blanket next door. Kayla's family had arrived the same morning, and the two of them had discovered they were both entering eighth grade in the fall.

Kayla turned the glass over in her palm. "You can't take that."

"Why not? It's just glass."

"There's a sign at the trailhead." Kayla pointed back toward the parking lot. "This whole beach is part of the national lakeshore. It says Leave No Trace on it. My mom made us read the whole thing twice. She's like that."

Jasmine had seen the sign but hadn't stopped. She walked back up the sand with Kayla and read it herself to verify what her friend claimed. The sign listed the outdoor ethics called Leave No Trace, organized as seven principles. Dispose of waste properly was one of them. Another was Leave What You Find. Under that heading it said not to remove rocks, plants, shells, or artifacts. So the sea glass counted. Even the driftwood her brother was stacking into a fort counted, at least the part about taking it home.

At first this seemed annoying but plausible once she thought about it. If every visitor took one shell or one stone, and hundreds of thousands of people came each summer, the beach would slowly get stripped. She couldn't see that happening from one afternoon, but the rule was the visible trace of it.

Here was the twist. When she got back to the umbrella, her brother's pockets were bulging. He opened his hand and showed her five white shells and one flat gray stone with a hole worn through the middle.

"For my room," he said.

"You have to put those back," Jasmine said.

"You got glass."

"I'm putting it back too." She held out her hand for the stone with the hole, because she had wanted that one herself a minute ago, and she was glad he had found it first so she wouldn't have to argue with herself. "It's called Leave What You Find. It's one of the seven."

He frowned at the stone, then at the water. "Can I keep it just for today?"

"Until we leave. Then it goes back on the sand."

They carried the shells and the stone and the sea glass down to the wet part of the beach, where the waves would reach them, and set them in a row above the foam. Her brother placed the stone last and patted it once. "Bye, rock."

Kayla, who had been carrying a perfect sand dollar behind her back the whole time, knelt and set it down at the end of the row.

"Your mom made you read the sign twice," Jasmine said.

"I know," Kayla said. "But I wanted to see if it counted for sand dollars."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
story:
Grandma Dot arrived on Saturday with one suitcase, one knitting bag, and one ear that, as she put it, "doesn't pull its weight anymore." Savannah had been given the air mattress in the den, and Grandma Dot got Savannah's bed, which meant for one whole week Savannah would wake up to the smell of coffee and the sound of the knitting needles clicking before sunrise.

The trouble started right away. Sunday morning, Savannah shouted from the kitchen, "Do you want eggs?" Grandma Dot shouted back, "Weeds? Why would I want weeds?" Savannah shouted louder, "EGGS!" and Grandma Dot said, "No need to yell, child, I'm not deaf." Except she sort of was, in one ear, and shouting was making everything worse somehow, which made no sense to Savannah at all. If a thing was too quiet, making it louder should fix it. That was just how sound worked.

On Monday, Savannah's mom sent them to the Saturday street market on a Monday, because that was the week it ran, with a list and twenty dollars. At the honey stall, a woman selling jars was chatting with everyone, and Savannah noticed something odd. When the woman turned sideways to reach a jar, Grandma Dot's smile went stiff and fake, the smile of someone guessing. But when the woman faced her directly and spoke at a normal volume, moving her lips plainly, Grandma Dot laughed at the actual joke. Savannah watched it happen three more times: at the tomato stall, at the bread table, and again with a kid selling pet treats who kept turning to point at a poster of a smiling rodent in a wheel while he talked.

"You're doing a science experiment with your face," said Julie, who had tagged along for the free samples. "You keep staring at your grandma's ears like they owe you money."

"I'm testing something," Savannah said. She devised a plan for the rest of the market: every single time she had something to say to Grandma Dot, she would walk around to her left side, stand where she could be seen, and speak clearly at a normal volume. Not once would she shout from a distance. If Grandma Dot understood her all morning, then facing a person with hearing loss and speaking plainly helped more than shouting did, and Savannah would have her answer.

So when Grandma Dot drifted toward the jam table and Savannah spotted her favorite, the pear-ginger, she didn't call out. She walked over, touched her sleeve, and said, "The pear-ginger is back here, and Julie says the samples are bigger if you compliment the farmer's hat."

Grandma Dot looked at her for a second, then grinned. "Now that," she said, "I heard every word of. You've got the makings of an eloquent negotiator, child. Let's go flatter that hat."

Julie was already asking the farmer whether his straw hat was handmade.

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
story:
Saturday morning drills ended in forty minutes, and George had promised his coach he would run the pick and roll right by then or lose the point guard spot for Monday's game. So he dragged Charlie and Lisa to the running track, because the painted lines there were almost symmetrical, square enough to stand in for a court.

"You practice basketball on a track?" Charlie said.

"Lines are lines," George said. "You stand at the curve, that's the top of the key. Lisa, you set the screen on my defender. Charlie, you play defense on me and shout what you're doing."

They ran it. Lisa planted herself beside Charlie, and George swept around her like she was a door swinging open. Charlie stayed with him. Fine. He passed back to Lisa, who popped a shot at an imaginary hoop and missed the water bottle they were using as the rim.

"Again," George said. "Faster."

They ran it five more times, and George's passes kept fluctuating between too soft and rocket hard, so Lisa's catches were a mess. He stopped, ball on his hip, thinking. The coach had said the same thing every practice: "George, you never look off the ball." He'd thought that just meant don't stare. But maybe the real problem was hidden. Maybe the defense was telling him something he wasn't reading.

"Charlie," George said, "this time both of you guard me. Trap me. Like the other team did Tuesday."

"What, leave Lisa totally alone?"

"Just do it."

The play started. Lisa screened, George curled, and both defenders crashed onto him, arms swarming the ball. His old habit screamed dribble backward. Instead he heard the coach's phrase in his head, spun, and there was Lisa, already rolling to the basket with nobody within ten feet. The pass came out easy, soft, perfect. Lisa laid the ball up over the water bottle and knocked it over.

"YES!" Lisa yelled, loud enough that a sprinter in lane three flinched and dropped the larva she'd been studying for her science project into the grass.

"So that's the whole trick," Charlie said, jogging back. "If we both go after you, she's open."

"That's the whole trick," George said, grinning. "Two on the ball, one pass, easy bucket. Monday is going to be so much fun."

"Twenty minutes left," Lisa said, setting the bottle upright. "Run it again."

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
story:
Charlie slid into her seat in the computer lab just as the bell finished ringing. Mr. Fraser had put the assignment on the board: build a spreadsheet of the class fund-raiser sales, add the column with SUM, and make a bar chart of each student's total. Charlie wanted hers done by the end of the period, because Yani had promised to trade her a bag of lemon chips for a look at the finished chart.

She typed the names down column A and the dollar amounts down column B, then pasted one more row from the note Yani had sent her, Gracie's total of fourteen dollars. In cell B12 she typed =SUM(B2:B10) and pressed Enter. The number that appeared was 128. She checked it against her paper list, where the total should have been 142.

"Your total's wrong," Yani said, leaning over from the next computer.

"I know it's wrong. I don't know why." Charlie clicked on each cell in the column, one at a time. When she got to B10, the cell with Gracie's fourteen, she noticed something in the formula bar. There were quotation marks around the number, like it was a word instead of a number. She looked at the alignment of the cells too. The other numbers sat on the right side of their cells, but this one sat on the left, the way words did.

"Mr. Fraser," she called, "can SUM skip a cell?"

"If the cell holds text, SUM skips it," Mr. Fraser said, and kept walking between the rows of desks.

Charlie had her idea, then. SUM skipped cells that held text, and this fourteen was being held as text, so it was being left out of the total. She tested it the simple way: she retyped the fourteen directly into B10, with no quotation marks anywhere. The total in B12 changed to 142, exactly what her paper list said. The bar chart updated at the same moment, and Gracie's bar grew taller than Yani's, which had not been true a second before.

"Hey," Yani said, staring at the chart. "Gracie beat me?"

"She beat you the whole time. The spreadsheet just didn't know it." Charlie highlighted the chart, copied it, and pasted it into a new sheet so she could show Gracie in the hallway. Then she held out her hand. "Chips first."

Yani dropped the bag on the keyboard. "That was worth it. You should write this down somewhere, so you remember."

Charlie opened a blank cell at the bottom and typed a short note to herself, the way you might summarize a whole afternoon in one line: check for numbers stored as text. She read it over, decided it was an authentic record of what had actually happened, and saved the file. On her way out, she waved the printed chart at Gracie, who was waiting by the water fountain.

"Fourteen dollars," Charlie said. "You owe me a high five."

story:
The letter p sat in Sara's piano book like a tiny spy, and she had played it loud for three straight weeks before Ms. Nwosu finally put her hand over the keys.

"Piano," Ms. Nwosu said, tapping the page.

"I am playing the piano," Sara said. "That's sort of the whole problem."

Ms. Nwosu laughed so hard she had to set down her tea. "The word, not the instrument. In music, piano means soft. Little p, quiet hands. And forte means loud." She spun the metronome like a top. "Now, again, and this time listen to yourself."

That was the trouble. Sara had never listened to herself. She had been too busy worrying about the notes, consuming the page one measure at a time while her hands sprinted ahead of her ears. She wanted more than anything to play "The Huntsman's Song" at the spring recital, and Alden, who had heard her practice, had said it sounded like a stampede of very determined cows.

At home that night, Sara tried an experiment. She folded a sticky note in half and wrote SOFT on it, then propped it on the music stand like a tiny road sign. The p in measure four was small and easy to ignore, but a big orange SOFT was not. She played the phrase. The sound came out gentle, almost secretive, like the huntsman sneaking up on something.

Then came measure eight, with the word forte stamped under the staff like a shout. She played it loud, and for the first time she noticed the difference in her own arms, loose for soft, weighty for loud, like shifting a backpack from one shoulder to both. The piece had a shape now. Quiet, loud, quiet again. It was a pattern, a secret code the composer had hidden in Italian.

The next lesson, Ms. Nwosu didn't say a word. She just pulled up a chair in the corner and listened, her fingers conducting little invisible waves in the air. When Sara finished, the room stayed silent for one second, which felt like an hour.

"Well," said Ms. Nwosu. "The cows have been sent to a nicer field."

Alden, waiting outside with his trumpet case, peeked in the door. "Was that actually you?"

"It was the p," Sara said, pointing at the page. "It means soft. It was right there the whole time, being tiny and quiet about it."

"Sort of like you before recital practice," Alden said, and then he ran for it, laughing, before she could swat him with the book.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
story:
Austin sat at the kitchen table with a mug of tea, a wad of tissues beside him, and his mother's thermometer on the counter. Three days home from school, and he was tired of being tired. He scrolled on his phone and found a message from Maina: "You missed the science fair meeting. Mr. Ong says pick a topic by Friday."

He typed back with one thumb. "Sick. Got any ideas."

"Pick something about colds, since you're an expert now," she wrote.

He almost laughed, which turned into a cough. Then he actually started thinking. His grandmother claimed the flu shot gave her a cold every winter, and she refused to get it again. His father said that was nonsense. Austin had never known who was right, and nobody at dinner would settle it. A science project might.

He opened the library site on his phone and searched. The first solid result stopped him cold, so to speak. More than 200 different viruses could cause the common cold. Two hundred. No wonder there was no single cold vaccine; the shot his grandmother blamed couldn't possibly cover all of them. He read further and learned that the most frequent cause was a group called rhinoviruses. He said the word out loud to the empty kitchen. "Rhinoviruses."

He started a note on his phone. He could classify the culprits into groups, list the big families, and put rhinoviruses at the top with the most cases. He found a line about how a famous, prestigious medical journal had published a study on cold viruses, and another paragraph mentioning an old controversy over whether vitamin C helped at all. He wrote both down, then texted Maina a list of what he had so far.

"Good," she answered, "but where's the question? Mr. Ong wants a question, not a report."

Austin stared at his notes. Then he remembered something. Last Friday, before he got sick, he had been at Reese's house, and Reese had been sniffling all through their game. Austin had teased him about it. He scrolled back through their messages until he found the one from Saturday morning: "Can't come today, my throat is destroyed." Austin's own sore throat had started Sunday.

He texted Reese. "Question. When did your cold start, like the exact day?"

"Friday I think? Why."

"So I got it from you." Austin grinned, then stopped. His own symptoms had shown up Sunday, and Reese had been sniffling Friday, which meant Reese caught it first, probably from school, not from Austin. But Austin had been fine until after the sleepover, and the timing fit. He typed, "For my science project. Patient zero. You're going in my notes."

Reese sent back a single word: "Rude."

Austin dragged the thermometer across the counter toward himself and took his temperature again, still writing with his other hand. 99.1. "Maina, tell Mr. Ong my question is: how do you track a cold back to its source?"

story:
Peyton raced down the hall toward the gym with her poster rolled under one arm, dodging a kid carrying a baking-soda volcano. The science fair opened in twenty minutes, and her project on neon was going to be the best one there. She had built a glowing sign with a battery and a small neon tube borrowed from her uncle's shop, and she planned to quiz everyone who stopped by.

"Let me see the poster," said Shania, catching up beside her. They found their assigned table near the door, and Peyton unrolled the poster and weighted the corners with erasers. At the top she had copied the box for neon from the periodic table, with its symbol Ne and the number 10.

A boy from another class, Avi, wandered over with his hands in his pockets. "Ten what?" he asked, pointing at the number. "Ten neutrons? Ten of something, but what?"

Peyton opened her mouth and then closed it again. She realized she had copied the box without ever asking what that small number meant, and her stomach dipped. Her whole poster was about neon, and she could not answer the first question someone asked. "I think it's called the atomic number," she said slowly, "but I don't actually know what that counts."

"Don't guess at people's posters," Shania said, but Peyton was already off her chair.

Mr. McKenzie, who ran the fair, had set up a giant periodic table banner along the back wall of the gym. Peyton drafted Avi and Shania to help her check every element box on it, moving systematically from hydrogen across the first row. "Hydrogen is 1," she said, tapping the box. "Helium is 2. Look, the numbers go up one at a time, all the way across."

"So it's counting something inside the atom," Shania said. "Something every atom of that element has."

They reached carbon, then oxygen, then fluorine, and each box matched the pattern. Peyton felt her pulse quicken, because a pattern that held every single time felt like a rule, not a coincidence. At the reference table by the wall sat an open chemistry textbook that Mr. McKenzie had left out for the judges. Peyton flipped until she found the periodic table chapter and ran her finger down the page. She read the line twice, then spun around.

"Avi! It's the protons," she said. "The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of every atom of that element. Hydrogen has one proton, helium has two, so neon, number ten, has ten protons in every single neon atom. In my tube, in the sign, in every neon sign in the whole world!"

Avi peered at the banner, then at her poster, checking for a contradiction between the two and finding none. "So carbon would be six protons," he said, "and oxygen would be eight. That's actually a cool trick."

When the judges reached her table an hour later, Peyton stood beside her glowing sign, pointed at the 10 in her copied box, and said, "Ten protons, in every atom of neon there is." The judge wrote something on her clipboard, and behind her, Shania gave both thumbs up.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
story:
The rumor reached Cole before the bus even stopped squeaking at the corner: Bentley said the Eiffel Tower was in Berlin, and anyone who disagreed was, in his words, "attacking his opinion." Cole slid into the seat across from Bentley and Olivier, who were already arguing over a half-eaten bag of chips.

"I looked it up last night for my France project," Olivier said, holding out his phone. "Paris. It's in Paris. Every source says Paris."

"Those are just sources," Bentley said, leaning back like the seat was a throne. "My opinion is that it's in Berlin, and opinions can't be wrong. That's the whole point of opinions."

Cole remembered standing in Mr. Russo's classroom two weeks earlier, holding his own half-finished essay about whether the school should ban pizza on Fridays. Mr. Russo had drawn a line down the whiteboard and asked which side of the line "my favorite lunch is pizza" belonged on, and which side "pizza costs three dollars" belonged on. One side of the line could be checked. The other side was just him. Cole had stared at that line for a long minute, feeling something click into place, and now, on the bus, he felt the same click.

"Wait," Cole said. "Say the tower part again."

"It's in Berlin," Bentley said. "My opinion."

"That's not an opinion, though. That's a claim." Cole pulled out his own phone. "Watch. I'm going to check it. If it says Paris, then your claim is false. If it says Berlin, I'll admit you're right." He typed the words into the search bar while Olivier leaned over his shoulder and Bentley scoffed at the window.

The screen loaded. Paris, France, in every result, with pictures Cole had seen a hundred times in Olivier's project folder.

"See?" Bentley said quickly. "Still my opinion."

"An opinion is like 'Berlin is a better city.' Nobody can check that, so it can't be false." Cole turned the phone toward him. "But 'The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin' is a wrong factual claim, not an opinion. It's a thing anybody can go look at, and it isn't where you said."

Bentley stared at the screen for a moment. Then a notorious scavenger of other people's snacks, he reached over and invaded Olivier's chip bag without asking. "Fine. But the part about Berlin being better, that one's mine."

"That one's all yours," Olivier said, yanking the bag away. "And so is this."

The bus lurched around the corner, and Cole slid the phone back into his pocket, grinning at the smear of chip dust Bentley left on the window.

story:
Beatrice had come to the community art studio to draw a street, and her street looked like it had been crushed by a giant. The buildings leaned inward at all the wrong angles, and the road shot off the paper like a runaway skateboard. She flattened the page with her palm, wondering if she should just crumple it now and dismiss the whole idea of perspective as a rumor invented by artists to torture eleven-year-olds.

"You look like you're drawing an earthquake," said Everly, sliding into the seat beside her.

"It's supposed to be Maple Street." Beatrice turned her pencil over and erased the left building entirely. "Ms. Rosen says the lines are supposed to meet somewhere, but I keep missing."

Ms. Rosen had pinned a poster on the wall that first day, a print of a painting from a church in Florence. It showed a vaulted ceiling, tall columns, a figure floating on a cross, and it looked as deep as a hallway, even though it was flat paint. Ms. Rosen had said only one thing about it, that the whole picture was organized toward a single point, and that a painter named Masaccio had made it around 1427, one of the earliest pictures ever built that way. Then she'd told them to figure the rest out themselves, which Beatrice had thought at the time was a kind of small rebellion against teaching. Now she wasn't so sure.

She got up and stood in front of the poster. Everly followed, chewing the end of a paintbrush. Beatrice raised her finger and set it on the ceiling line on the left side, then traced it slowly toward the middle of the picture. She did the same with the right ceiling line. They met. She tried the lines in the floor, the lines in the steps, the edges of the arch. Every single one ran to the same spot, just beneath the floating figure, like all the beams in the world had agreed to shake hands in one place.

"It's like they're all sneaking off to the same secret meeting," Everly said.

Beatrice hurried back to her table. She drew a small dot in the middle of a fresh page, then drew lines out from it like spokes, and laid her buildings and her road along them. The street ran away from her, narrowing, tidy, almost real. She checked each edge against the dot with the meticulous care of someone defusing a very small bomb, because she had learned that one lazy line ruined everything. Her last drawing had taught her that much.

"Mine still looks like a landslide," Everly said behind her, holding up a page of wobbly buildings.

"Put a dot first," Beatrice said. "Everything goes to the dot." She tapped her own vanishing point twice, then leaned over Everly's shoulder with her pencil. "Trace your ceiling. Just watch where it wants to go."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
story:
Jackson sat in the third row of the auditorium with his hands folded, waiting for his turn at the microphone. Twenty-two contestants, one impartial judge at the scorer's table, and a list of words nobody had seen. Two rows back, Marwan was mouthing letters to himself, and near the piano, Axl gave Jackson a small thumbs-up.

The week before, Jackson had nearly quit studying. He had missed "bite" three times in a row, adding an extra e or dropping the silent one, and he'd slammed his word list on the kitchen table. Why did English need letters that did nothing? His mother said English was just strange and he should memorize. But memorizing felt like guessing, and Jackson hated guessing. So he'd gone to the library and pulled down a fat book about the history of English, and there he found something that changed everything. Between about 1400 and 1700, the vowel sounds had shifted, and this had happened after spellings had already started to become fixed. The book called it the Great Vowel Shift. The words hadn't changed; the way people said them had. The silent e in "bite" was like a fossil, a sound that had once been there, preserved on paper while mouths moved on.

Sitting in the auditorium now, Jackson tested his idea against every word the judge gave the other contestants. "Name," said the judge, and Jackson deduced that the a had probably once sounded different, more like "nah-meh," before the shift dragged it upward. "Clean." "Beak." Each one fit. If the pattern held, then strange spellings weren't tricks; they were leftovers, and leftovers could be reasoned about instead of memorized.

"Jackson Reyes."

He walked to the microphone. The impartial judge, a gray-haired woman who had congratulated and eliminated contestants with exactly the same nod, leaned toward her list.

"Your word is deduce."

Jackson almost laughed. "Deduce. D-E-D-U-C-E. Deduce."

"Correct."

The next round took Marwan, who added an s to the end of "vaccine," and Jackson felt a twist of guilt, because last winter he had told Marwan the spelling bee was a waste of a Saturday and Marwan had signed up anyway, alone. Jackson hadn't even wished him luck until this morning. Maybe he'd been a bad friend. Maybe Marwan had just needed to want it for himself.

Round five came down to Jackson and a girl from another school. The judge cleared her throat.

"Your word is height."

H-E-I before the ght, or just E? Jackson closed his eyes and saw the library book, the long chapter about vowels wandering while spelling stood still. The i in height had once sounded different, longer, like "heeth." The spelling was holding onto that old sound, so the i came first, and then, because that's how the letters had been fixed, the e after it.

He opened his eyes. "Height. H-E-I-G-H-T. Height."

The bell stayed silent. The judge smiled, and somewhere behind him, Axl was on his feet.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
story:
Ethan spread the photocopied diary pages across the library table like treasure maps, which was pretty much what they were. Mr. Bélanger had pulled the settler's diary from the archives box that morning, and Ethan had claimed it before anyone else could. His project was due Friday: use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. The diary's writer, a farmer named Josiah Cole, went on and on about cheap land and a fresh start, which was perfect. Except for one line. "Reached the river crossing on the fourteenth of April," it said, "the very day the papers said the ice broke."

"That's weird," said Mathilde, leaning over his shoulder. She slid the microfilm reel of the old newspaper toward her. "The Herald says the ice broke on April ninth. Five days earlier."

"Maybe he wrote it wrong," said Lee, dropping into the chair across from them with a thud. "People make stuff up in diaries all the time. My cousin writes in hers that she's going to be famous."

"He didn't necessarily make it up." Ethan tapped the diary page. "Maybe the newspaper got it wrong. That's a hypothetical. Either one could be the mistake. We can't just guess." He sat back, thinking. If the diary said something the paper contradicted, there had to be a way to check which one was telling the truth. Then it hit him. "Wait. Mr. Bélanger said historians test a diary against other sources. Letters, newspapers, government records. We have the newspaper. We need the other two."

Mathilde grabbed the folder of Cole's family letters while Lee prioritized speed over neatness and dumped the entire government records box onto the table. They had twenty minutes before the bell. Ethan read fast, skimming for anything about April, the river, the ice. A letter from Cole's wife to her sister, dated April eleventh, mentioned that her husband had been stuck at the crossing for two days waiting for the ferry crews to arrive. Two days after the ninth. That matched the newspaper.

"Government records," Lee said, breathless, flipping a page. "Ferry ledger! Look, ferry service started on the tenth, because of the ice." He shoved the book across the table so hard it slid into the dictionary shelf with a bang.

Ethan grinned so wide his face hurt. Three sources agreed, and the diary was the odd one out. Cole had probably written his entries days later, from memory, and gotten the date wrong. "So we can still use the diary for why he moved west," Ethan said, already writing. "We just note that the dates were checked against other sources, and the newspaper was right." He underlined his next sentence twice.

Mathilde read it over his shoulder and nodded. "Mr. Bélanger is going to lose his mind."

"He's going to put it on the bulletin board," Lee said. "I'm calling it right now."

story:
Autumn stood in the doorway of Room 12 with her schedule pressed flat against her binder, watching students who all seemed to know exactly which desk was theirs. The town was only three hours from her old one, but it might as well have been on the far side of a prism, and everything here split her into a stranger. At her old school she had sat with the same four people every day at lunch until the table felt like it belonged to them. Here she had nobody, and lunch was forty minutes long.

She noticed something during second period, though. The girl across the aisle, Anita, kept whispering about a roster with another girl, checking names off. When the bell rang, Autumn leaned over. "What's the list for?"

"Chess club," Anita said. "We meet Tuesdays and Thursdays at lunch in Mr. Whitehead's room. We're still short two players for the tournament, and I want us to actually field a full team this year." She hesitated, then added, "You could sign up. We take beginners."

Autumn had never played chess in her life. But she thought about it through math class. In her old town, her best friend Vincent had lived two doors down, and their friendship had grown because they saw each other every single day, whether they planned to or not. Regular contact was the thing. A club met on a schedule with the same people, over and over, all of them caring about the same activity. That was how a friendship got time to grow. A one-time invitation to sit somewhere would not replicate that. She needed something that repeated.

At lunch she found Mr. Whitehead's room and wrote her name at the bottom of the roster. "I don't really know how to play," she admitted.

"Anita will teach you," Mr. Whitehead said from the window, where he was watering a spider plant. "She's the most assertive teacher in the club, and I mean that nicely."

Anita was already setting up a board at the corner table, waving her over. "Pawns first. Move this one forward two."

A boy named Vincent from her science class slid into the seat across from them and said, "I heard there was a new player. I need somebody at my level."

"There is nobody at your level," Anita said, "but she's closer than I am."

Autumn laughed, and Anita showed her the pawn moves twice more, patient as a Sunday. By the end of lunch they had decided Autumn would practice the knight on Thursday, and Anita had promised to bring her spare board to the tournament.

On Tuesday the following week, Autumn walked into the room and Anita moved her backpack off the chair beside her without being asked. "Your seat," Anita said. "You're on my team now."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
story:
Payton peeled a paper-thin layer from the inside of an onion and laid it on her glass slide, the way Ms. Choi had shown the class that morning. One drop of iodine, then the coverslip. She lowered the little square of glass flat onto the specimen and pressed it down with her thumb, because pressing seemed like the way to make it stay.

Under the microscope, the field filled with round shapes, dark circles with black rims, dozens of them, stacked like coins. Payton turned the coarse focus knob slowly. She drew the circles in her lab notebook and labeled the first one nucleus, because a nucleus should be round and dark, shouldn't it? Something nagged at her, though. The circles were too perfect. And they were everywhere, even in places where no onion skin should be.

"Those aren't cells," said Harper, leaning over from the next stool. "I think they're air bubbles. My slide looked like that too, last period."

"Bubbles." Payton sat back. "Then where are my cells?"

"Under the bubbles, probably. Or squashed."

Payton remembered fourth grade then, the afternoon she and her cousin had tried to install a clear screen protector on a tablet. They had pressed it flat, all at once, and trapped a dozen dusty bubbles underneath, big obvious circles that she had mistaken at first for fingerprints. Her cousin had peeled it off and tried again, laying down one edge first and letting the rest settle slowly. The bubbles had slid out ahead of it, like they were being pushed aside. She had never thought about why. It had just worked.

She looked at her slide. She had pressed the coverslip flat, all at once. Same mistake.

Princess, two stools down, was struggling with her own coverslip, tweezers in hand. "Mine keeps sliding off."

"Hold on," Payton said. "Watch this." She took a fresh piece of onion skin, added the iodine, then lifted a clean coverslip with the tweezers and set it down at an angle, one edge touching the liquid first, and lowered the rest slowly. It settled over the specimen like a door closing. When she looked through the eyepiece, the dark-rimmed circles were gone. Instead she saw boxes in rows, brick-shaped, tidy as a garden wall, each one edged with a clear line, and here and there a small dark dot.

"There they are," she said. "Cell wall, and the dot's the nucleus."

Princess copied the angled lowering, one edge first, and her slide cleared up too. Ms. Choi walked past, glanced at Payton's notebook, and slid the fine focus a hair to the left.

"That's the cell membrane, right inside the wall," Ms. Choi said, tapping the page. "Draw it in."

Payton drew the thin inner line on every box. It was not trivial, that one careful edge-first lowering, and it was not some equation she could copy off the board. It was just a small thing you did with your hands, and it made all the difference.

"Next slide, I'm doing it without the tweezers," Princess said.

"Race you," said Payton, already peeling the onion.

story:
Arianna slid off her bike at the Sunoco station just as the storm clouds rolled in, and the first thing she noticed was the handwritten sign taped to the cooler: bottled water, two dollars. Yesterday it had been ninety-nine cents. She had fifteen dollars in her pocket from collecting cans all week, and she needed twelve bottles for her soccer team's tournament tomorrow, which meant she suddenly needed twenty-four dollars instead of twelve.

"Nobody's going to pay that," she told Andrea, who was leaning against the ice machine. Andrea shook her head and pointed at the parking lot. A man was carrying out an armful of bottles, and behind him a woman was filling a whole basket. The radio had warned that the storm might knock out the town's water for a day or two, and everyone wanted bottled water at once, while the store had only its one small cooler of it.

Arianna did a quick census of the cooler, counting what was left and who took what. In ten minutes, six people bought water at two dollars, but four people picked it up, saw the sign, and put it back. Yesterday, she remembered, the cooler had sold maybe ten bottles at ninety-nine cents all afternoon, because back then there was plenty and nobody was worried. Now the water was scarce, the price was up, and fewer people were willing to buy it. She whispered her discovery to Andrea like it was a secret code. "When the price goes up, people buy less. When it goes down, they buy more. If nothing else changes."

"My sister calls that the law of demand," Andrea confessed. "She learned it in high school. She raised her lemonade price from fifty cents to a dollar and only half as many people bought it."

Arianna's problem still stood, though. She needed twelve bottles and couldn't afford twenty-four dollars. Then she spotted the shelf above the cooler, stacked with gallon jugs of spring water that nobody was touching. The jugs were still ninety-nine cents each because, she guessed, people wanted the easy little bottles. She grabbed three jugs, plus two bottles for the goalies, and paid eleven dollars and change.

As she wheeled her bike out with the jugs bungee-corded to the rack, Ms. Berg pulled up in her truck and headed straight for the cooler. Arianna pointed up at the shelf. "Jugs are half the price and nobody's fighting over them."

story:
Anna lay on the living room carpet with three campaign posters spread out in front of her, a glass of juice sweating on the coffee table above her head. Gabriela was running for student council against a boy named Devon, whose posters had appeared overnight like mushrooms after rain. Every single one showed Devon doing ordinary things: eating a sandwich in the cafeteria, tying his shoe by the gym, laughing with a group of kids Anna had never actually seen him talk to. Gabriela's posters, by contrast, listed her ideas in bullet points, and nobody looked at them twice.

"He's going to demolish me," Gabriela said from the couch, where she was cutting out more bullet points. "Everyone keeps saying he seems so normal. So relatable."

"His plan is a mascot and 'better vibes,'" said Hallie, who was sitting cross-legged on the rug, sorting markers by color whether anyone asked her to or not. "My brother voted for him already and the election's not until Friday. He said, and I quote, Devon eats lunch like us."

Anna stared at the poster of Devon with his sandwich. He wasn't doing anything. He was just sitting there, being a regular person, and somehow that was working better than an entire page of Gabriela's proposals about the broken water fountain outside the library. She flipped the poster over, then flipped it back. "He's not winning because of the sandwich," she said slowly. "He's winning because of the sandwich."

"That's what I said," said Gabriela.

"No, I mean it's a technique." Anna scrambled up and dug through her backpack for the media literacy worksheet Mr. Anderson had handed out on Friday, mostly crumpled, still faintly smelling of the bottom of her locker. She smoothed it on the coffee table and ran her finger down the list until she found it. "It's called the plain-folks technique. It presents a politician or a company as ordinary, everyday people, so the audience trusts them as one of us. That's Devon's whole campaign. He's advertising his own normalness."

Hallie capped a marker with great ceremony. "So we make you look normal too? You are normal. Painfully normal."

Gabriela did not thank her for this. But she did grab a fresh poster board, and while Anna held the juice glass safely out of the way, Gabriela drew herself tying her shoe, with one small difference: taped beside it, a strip of paper reading "AND a new water fountain by October." Then she drew herself holding a wrench, which she had never held in her life, and decided that was fine.

They hung the posters in the hallway before first period, and by lunch three people had asked Gabriela about the water fountain, and one person asked Devon what his plan was. Devon said better vibes. Hallie reported this at the living room strategy session that afternoon, sitting exactly where she had been the day before, markers resorted. "He panicked a little," she said. "It was beautiful."

story:
William had typed the message three times and deleted it twice. "Okay. See you there." He hit send anyway, because Zack had asked twice whether he was coming to the robotics club party, and ignoring it seemed worse.

The next morning in the computer lab, Zack sat two rows away and did not turn around. That alone was strange, because Zack usually talked through the whole class until Mr. Hosseini gave him the look. Today Zack just typed, his shoulders stiff, his face indifferent to the joke Artin was telling about a laptop that caught an infection from a bad download and started sneezing files everywhere. Artin laughed at his own joke, then leaned toward William and lowered his voice.

"It's you he's mad at," Artin whispered. "He showed me your text at lunch. He thinks you don't want to come. He said it sounded, like, angry." Artin had his own plan for the period, a poster for the coding contest he was desperate to conquer, but he kept glancing over at Zack instead of working on it. "Fix it before Friday, or the whole club party is going to be weird."

William stared at his screen. His message had been two words. Two words, and one of them was okay. How could okay sound angry? He opened his sent messages and read it again. Then he opened the message he had sent to Artin the same night, about the game they were both playing: "no way, that boss took me four tries lol." No period. No capital letters. It looked friendly. His message to Zack had a period after every sentence, sitting there like a little closed door.

He had an idea. He typed the exact same message twice and sent one to Artin as a test: "Okay." and then "okay". Artin read them, frowned, and typed back, "the first one sounds like you're mad at me?? the second one's fine." William's pulse ticked faster. It was the period. Same words, different dot, different feeling. He searched the school database, feeling like a detective, and found a news article about a small 2016 study by Binghamton University researchers. They had found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one. He read it twice. It wasn't just Zack being dramatic. It was a real thing that had been measured.

He typed fast: "zack. i was NOT mad. i just used periods. a 2016 study from binghamton university says texts with periods at the end actually seem less sincere than the same text without one. no period this time, see" He sent it without any punctuation at the end at all, then sat very still, watching Zack's screen from across the room.

Zack's typing stopped. His shoulders shook once, then again. He turned around and held up his phone, showing a new message he had typed: "okay okay. bring snacks"

"Deal," William said, and behind them Mr. Hosseini cleared his throat and pointed at the clock.

story:
Sawyer's first pet was a gray cat named Biscuit, and by Saturday afternoon Biscuit was missing. He had wedged the window screen loose, and when Sawyer went to close it against the coming precipitation, the screen swung free and the porch was empty.

Two days earlier, at the shelter, Sawyer had filled out the paperwork while Ajay peered into the kennels. Ajay wanted to be a vet someday, so he read every information card out loud, warning Sawyer that one kitten's file mentioned a spider bite, "probably not venomous, but still." When the volunteer mentioned that Biscuit had a microchip, Ajay had nodded like a professional. Sawyer remembered thinking the chip sounded like a tiny tracker, the kind in spy movies.

Now he opened the app on his phone and searched for a map of Biscuit. He found nothing but ads. He called Ajay, who biked over in eleven minutes with a binder of vet facts he kept for fun. "It doesn't work like that," Ajay said, flipping pages. "A microchip has no GPS. It can't track where an animal is. It only gives its ID number when a scanner is held close." Sawyer slumped onto the porch steps. "So it's useless." "No," Ajay said. "It's useless for finding. It's for proving. When somebody finds him, a shelter scans the chip and they know he's yours."

They crawled through wet grass with a flashlight. Behind a stack of flowerpots, two eyes flashed green. Biscuit hissed, then crept into Sawyer's arms. Eleanor leaned forward between the front seats as the family car rolled toward the school gym, her new shoes already pinching. "Faster, Dad, Maksim said the line forms before seven."

Her dad laughed and stayed exactly at the speed limit. "It'll sustain your social life if we arrive alive."

The gym thundered before they even opened the doors. Inside, the DJ had stacked his speakers taller than the basketball hoop, and everyone crowded onto the floor right in front of them, dancing in a knot of elbows and glow sticks. Maksim and Kaylee waved Eleanor over from that exact spot.

"Best bass is right here," Maksim shouted, pointing at the speakers.

Eleanor started toward them, then stopped. Her ears already felt fuzzy from the doorway. She cupped her hands around her mouth. "Don't you think it's weird that we have to yell from here? If we're yelling to be heard, doesn't that mean it's really loud?"

Kaylee shrugged and kept dancing. Maksim leaned closer so she could hear him. "It's a dance. It's supposed to be loud."

But Eleanor had read something on her brother's phone last week, and it was nagging at her. She tried an experiment. She walked backward, one step at a time, until she could speak at a normal volume without straining. That felt like a clue. If the noise dropped off that much in a few meters, then the kids pressed against the speakers were getting the full blast, the whole notorious wall of it.

"Come back to the front!" Kaylee called.

"Watch this instead," Eleanor said. She waved them over to the far side near the water table, where the music was still huge but her voice worked normally. "If we can talk here, it's loud enough to dance and not so loud it's wrecking us."

Maksim grumbled, but Kaylee followed, and by the third song even Maksim admitted the far side had more room for his ridiculous spinning move.

The next morning, Eleanor's dad drove her to Maksim's house to return a jacket she'd borrowed. Maksim stood on his porch with his hands pressed over his ears. "I stood near the front for the last hour," he said, wincing. "My ears are still ringing. It's called tinnitus, my cousin told me on the phone. Eleanor's stomach dropped even as her brain lit up. That was the exact thing she'd read. The ringing wasn't just an after-effect; it was a warning sign. "So my backward-walking test was actually a real rule," she said. "Far enough away to talk normally, no ringing."

"Next dance," Maksim said, "I'm starting where you started. Water table side, no arguments." He climbed into the car, hands still hovering near his ears, and pointed down the street. "Drive past the school. I want to measure the distance with my steps."

story:
Antoine had been staring at the same paragraph for so long that the words had started to look like a fence. Ms. Park had assigned each student one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and his was freedom of expression, which sounded like the easiest one until he actually read it. His job was to explain it in his own words at the front of the class, and his own words currently amounted to "you can say stuff." He assumed a better version would arrive if he kept staring. It did not.

The problem arrived before the better version did. At lunch, Frank was holding court by the vending machines, announcing that freedom of expression meant anyone could say anything to anyone, anytime, including telling the vice principal his tie looked like a dead squid. "Charter, baby," Frank said. "It's the foundation of this country."

Paislee, who kept her social studies binder on her lap even while eating pizza, flipped it open. "Read section 1," she said, shoving the binder at him. "Out loud."

Frank sighed the sigh of a boy being handed homework during lunch, but he read it. "Section 1 of the Charter says the rights are subject to reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society." He paused. "That's a lot of words."

"That's the whole point," Paislee said. "Rights have limits if the limits can be justified."

Antoine chewed on this along with his sandwich. The squid-tie comment, he reasoned, probably was not a limit anyone could justify. It was just rude. But shouting fire in a crowded gym, or wearing a shirt that said something aggressive toward a specific kid, might be different. There was a rule under the rule, like wiring hidden inside a wall. He wanted to test it.

In grade four, he remembered, a kid on his soccer team had gotten a red card for yelling at the referee and then claimed the coach couldn't tell him what to say because of "rights." The coach had made him run laps, and the rights defense had not gone well. At the time Antoine had assumed the coach was just mean. Now it seemed the coach might have been onto something.

On presentation day, Antoine stood at the front with one index card, which he did not look at. "Freedom of expression means the government can't stop you from speaking your mind," he said. "But it isn't a free pass. The limits have to be reasonable, and they have to be justified in a free and democratic society. So Frank can say the vice principal's tie looks like a dead squid." He paused. "Whether he should is a different section."

Ms. Park wrote something on her clipboard. Frank raised his hand and asked, "Is there a section on dead squids?"

"Sit down, Frank," said Ms. Park.

story:
Hazel stood at the counter of the bank with her savings statement flat in front of her. She had been putting away birthday money for two years so she could buy a kayak, because Lee had promised to take her paddling in the estuary near his uncle's house once she had her own boat. The statement showed a line called interest, and the number next to it was bigger than she remembered.

"Can I ask about this?" she said to the teller. "Last year the interest was six dollars and something. Now it says seven fifty. I didn't put any money in."

The teller turned the paper toward her. "That's compound interest. Interest is paid on your balance plus the interest already earned."

"So the interest itself starts earning interest," Hazel said slowly, reading the numbers again.

"That's it exactly."

Hazel pulled a pencil from her backpack and did the arithmetic right there on the back of the statement. Simple interest, the way she had imagined it in her head, would pay the same amount every year, because it was always calculated on her original deposit. Compound interest paid on everything, so each year's payment was a little bigger than the last. She worked it out over five years, the way Ms. Wilson had shown them to test an idea in science class. The compound column beat the simple column by enough to matter, even though she added nothing to either one.

She texted Lee from the bench by the doors. "Guess what. My money is making money on its own money."

He wrote back, "That sounds fake."

"Come see the paper. I have two whole columns."

On Monday she showed the statement to Alyssia at lunch, and Alyssia tried to provoke an argument by insisting the bank was just being generous. Hazel shook her head and pointed at the line where the balance had grown. The interest from year one was sitting inside that balance, and year two's interest had been calculated on all of it, proof or not enough for Alyssia, who still frowned at the numbers.

Hazel walked home feeling buoyant, almost as if she were already out on the water. At her desk she started a new page. At the top she wrote "Year Three," and under it she began to calculate.

The gift worked even better. He turned the cookie box over in his hands like it was treasure and said he would share it with his wife. Alexis's stomach dropped. She tried to figure out what had just happened, running through possibilities like cards. It wasn't the noise. It wasn't the gesturing. It was the chopsticks, she realized. It was where they were standing. She remembered the incense sticks her grandmother lit at her grandfather's photo, thin and upright in a little dish, and the cold feeling of that memory lined up perfectly with the look on Mr. Yamamoto's face. "Khaled," she whispered, "lay them across the bowl. Trust me." He did, slowly, like he was defusing a bomb. Emerson leaned in. "Wait, why?" "It looks like incense," Alexis murmured. "You know, offered to the dead." Khaled's ears turned red as the lanterns.

Mr. Yamamoto came back with the teapot and, just like that, the cloud lifted. He topped off their cups and even chuckled at Khaled's volcano story, which Khaled nervously restarted from the beginning. Later, when the tempura arrived, Alexis watched Khaled lay his chopsticks neatly across his bowl every single time he paused, careful as a surgeon. "This table manner thing is controversial," he muttered, "in my house we just have forks." Emerson snorted so hard that rice nearly made a second escape. Alexis raised her teacup. "To ambassadors," she said, and three cups clinked over the steaming bowls.

story:
Victor sat at the back table in the art room, smudging pencil lines with the side of his hand. Ms. Augustin had told the class to draw a street that looked like it went somewhere, and Victor's street did not. His road edges spread apart as they went back, like a river getting wider instead of thinner.

"You got the chronic slouch again," Adelina said from the next stool, tapping his paper. "Your road's all floppy."

Victor leaned over his page. He had a ruler, and he had an idea. If the road was supposed to get smaller as it went back, then the two edges had to aim somewhere. He laid the ruler along his left edge and slid the pencil along it, extending the line onto a spare sheet clipped behind the drawing. He did the same with the right edge. The two lines crossed at one dot near the top of the spare sheet. Then he extended the sidewalk lines too. One of them crossed the same dot. The other two wandered off to different places entirely.

He looked across the room at Caden's drawing, the one Ms. Augustin had taped to the board as an example. Caden was a veteran of three summer art camps and had drawn a street with shopfronts and streetlights, and everything on it looked like it was actually sinking into the paper. Victor borrowed a viewfinder from the supply shelf and held it up, sighting across the room like a pirate. The ceiling lines above the windows, the shelf edges, even the baseboard all ran toward him in slanted directions. When he marked those slants lightly on a scrap, they pointed at one height, the height of his own eyes.

He went back to Caden's drawing and checked the streetlight on the left against the one on the right, the second-story windows against the doors. With his ruler he found every one of them. "They all go to one point," he said.

"Told you," Caden said from across the room without looking up. "Vanishing point. Everything sits on the horizon line, at your eye level."

Victor erased his floppy road. He drew a straight line across the page where his eye level would be, picked a point on it, and ran every edge toward that point from there. When Adelina and Caden argued about whose turn it was at the good pencil sharpener, he stepped in and settled it with a coin flip before Ms. Augustin could come over, which kept everyone drawing.

At the end of class Ms. Augustin walked the rows. She stopped at Victor's table and picked up the spare sheet, the one with the crossing lines and the dot. "This is the better drawing," she said, and pinned it to the board above Caden's.

Maelie had promised herself she would not hide in the back room, but by ten o'clock she was still sorting soup cans into crates, and she could hear Mary up front laughing with people in the serving line. Ms. Kamau, who ran the kitchen, patted the crates as she passed. "Pantry first, serving later," she said. "We can't postpone the pantry, or lunch doesn't happen." Maelie stacked another can and thought that was the kind of thing adults said to make chores sound important.

Then a truck rumbled into the alley, and Farhan came sprinting from the loading dock with rain dripping off his sleeves. "It's like a monsoon out there," he said, shaking water onto the floor. "Maelie, come look. That truck isn't from here. The plates say Ohio, but the side says the same thing as our truck."

Maelie followed him to the dock. Their own truck, the one that came every morning, had a green and blue logo on it with the words Feeding America. The new truck, wet and mud-splashed, had the exact same logo. Both drivers were rolling a ramp down together like they did this every day.

"That's weird," Maelie said. "Why would two trucks from different cities have the same logo?"

Farhan shrugged. "Maybe somebody copied it."

Maelie didn't think so. She went to find Ms. Kamau, who was ladling stew at the counter, and asked her straight out. Ms. Kamau smiled without stopping the ladle. "Feeding America is a nationwide network of more than 200 food banks," she said. "We're all one team, coast to coast." Then she called to the next person in line, because the line was long and getting longer.

Maelie stood there turning it over. A network. More than 200. That meant this kitchen in her town and that freezer in Ohio were connected somehow, like plugs in the same outlet. She had a theory, and she wanted to test it, so she marched back to the alley where the drivers were hauling boxes. "Excuse me," she said to the Ohio driver. "Did you come all this way because somebody needed something?"

The driver, a big woman with a whistle around her neck, grinned. "Our freezer broke last night. Called it in, and the closest kitchen with space was you. Forty tubs of soup. You good for it?"

Maelie checked with Ms. Kamau, then pointed the driver to the walk-in cooler. Farhan grabbed a dolly, and together they wheeled tub after tub inside, Farhan pretending each one weighed a thousand pounds. When they finished, he begged Ms. Kamau for a job up front instead of the pantry, because, he admitted quietly, he wanted to meet people, not just cans. She handed him a hairnet and a tray of rolls.

Back inside, Maelie carried two extra pots of soup to the serving line, and Mary waved her over to help ladle. An old man at the counter held out his bowl, and Maelie filled it to the brim, ladle steady, steam rising between them.

"Extra scoop today?" he asked.

"Freezer broke in Ohio," Maelie said. "You're eating soup from out of state."

He looked at her to see if she was joking, then at the full bowl, and laughed so hard the soup rippled.

story:
Alexis stood in aisle three of Ferris Pharmacy, staring at a wall of deodorants shaped like rocket ships and ice cream cones. Her mother had sent her in alone with ten dollars while she waited in the car with her phone. That was a vote of confidence, Alexis told herself, though her armpits had been voting loudly all through gym class, and Melia had whispered "deodorant, dude" during push-ups. The embarrassment had followed Alexis all day like a smell, which, she realized, was exactly the problem.

She grabbed the shiniest one on the shelf, something called Arctic Blast with a polar bear riding a snowboard on the label, and marched to the register before she could think twice. The cashier rang it up, and Alexis was already out the door when she noticed the price. Eleven dollars forty-nine. In the passenger seat she turned the thing over and found, printed on the back like a dare, the words COOLING SENSATION, FEEL THE FREEZE. Her mother raised an eyebrow but said nothing, which was somehow worse. At home Alexis tested it, and it felt like her armpits had been attacked by a fire extinguisher. It stung for an hour. She sat on her bed with her arms out like a scarecrow and thought about how she had chosen it. She hadn't planned. She had just grabbed.

Niko had left a library book in her backpack from last weekend, a book about the brain, and she opened it to escape the sting. On a page about teenagers she found a paragraph that stopped her cold. The prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties. She read it twice. "The prefrontal cortex," she said out loud to her scarecrow arms, "still under construction. Like the intersection by school."

On Monday she told Melia and Niko the whole thing at lunch, arms waving. "So it's not that I'm dumb," she said. "It's that the planning part of my brain is literally still being built, all the way into my twenties." Niko squinted. "So next time, plan before you grab?" Alexis considered that, because she had been hoping for more of an excuse and less of an assignment. "Fine," she said. "But I get until I'm twenty."

That afternoon she walked back to Ferris Pharmacy with her mother, returned the Arctic Blast, and took her time. She read three labels, compared prices, and picked a plain white stick that cost five dollars and promised nothing but working. Her mother paid, and Alexis carried the little bag out into the sunlight feeling strangely buoyant. "Look at that," her mother said. "Smart shopper." Alexis held the bag up like a trophy. "Growing brain," she said.
