story:
Leah stood in the dairy aisle holding two yogurts, but she wasn't really looking at them. She was looking at the calculator in her other hand, the one she'd brought from home in her back pocket. Her mother had said they could stay after shopping for ten minutes, and ten minutes was exactly what she needed.

The problem had started in math class. Ms. Suzuki had put two savings accounts on the board and asked which one would hold more money after five years. Leah had guessed the simple interest account, because five percent of forty dollars was two dollars, and two dollars times five years was ten dollars, so fifty dollars total. Joey had agreed with her. Nico had said "compound" and then refused to explain why, which made Leah suspect he didn't actually know.

"So what's the yogurt for?" Joey asked, sliding his cart alongside hers. He'd come with his own mother and had drifted over the moment he spotted Leah.

"Nothing. My mom wants the one with live cultures." Leah turned the cup so he could see the label. "It says microbes, billions of them, right in there."

"Great, invisible bugs in my breakfast." Joey picked up a granola bar instead and studied the price like it mattered.

Leah typed while she talked. "Okay, simple interest first. Forty, plus five percent, five times. Fifty dollars." Then she found the key with the little raised box on it, the power key Ms. Suzuki had mentioned only in passing. Forty times one point zero five, that was the first year, forty-two dollars. She could multiply that by one point zero five four more times, or she could try the shortcut. She typed 1.05, pressed the power key, then 5, and multiplied by 40.

The screen said 51.05.

"That's it?" Joey leaned over her shoulder. "A dollar and five cents more? I thought compound interest was supposed to be exciting."

"After five years it's a dollar. But it's not a straight line," Leah said. She changed the 5 to a 10 and pressed equals. Sixty-five dollars and nineteen cents. With simple interest it would only be sixty. She tried 20 years and got over a hundred and five, more than double what simple interest would give. "Every year the interest gets interest on top of it, so it keeps bending upward. Ten years, fifteen dollars extra. Twenty years, twenty-five extra. It speeds up."

"See, that's why I don't trust banks," Joey said. "They're biased toward the fancy math."

"They're biased toward the money, the math is just honest." Leah pocketed the calculator and dropped both yogurts into her mother's cart. "I'm texting Nico. He was right and he doesn't even know why."

"Tell him the invisible microbes helped," Joey said, and pushed his cart toward the checkout.

Alexandra pressed her nose to the glass case in the history-of-medicine hall and read the little card twice. Inside the case sat a glass flask with a neck that curved down and then up, like a swan trying to look at its own shoulder. The card said that Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long S-shaped necks, and the broth stayed free of microbes because dust and germs got trapped in the bend of the neck. She read that last part out loud, softly, to nobody.

"You've been standing there for ten minutes," Adam said, appearing beside her with two candy sticks from the gift shop. He offered her one. "The planetarium line was too long, so I figured you'd be somewhere weird."

"Last week my soup went bad," Alexandra said. "For the science fair. I made two jars of the same soup. The sealed one stayed fine, and the one I left open grew this grey film on top. Emmie caught up with them, out of breath. "Ms. Farah said to find you before the demonstration. Also, what's a swan-neck flask doing in the medicine hall?"

Alexandra pointed at the bend. "The bad stuff gets trapped right there, in the curve. The broth behind it stays clean." She frowned at her own memory of the jar, the grey film, the smell she had tried to forget. She had thrown it out right away, and now she wished she hadn't, because she would never know whether the film had come through the loose lid or from something already in the soup. Maybe she'd boiled it badly. Maybe she hadn't boiled it at all, just heated it. She couldn't remember which pot she'd used.

"So what's your guess?" Emmie asked.

Emmie grinned. "So break it."

Alexandra held them up to the case, comparing her mental picture of the soup jars with the swan neck in front of her. "If my guess about the boiling is right, then the juice in the open bottle should be fine either way, because it was sealed at the factory when it was clean. "That's kind of radical," Adam said, "testing soup rules with my juice."

"You'll persevere," Emmie told him. "You're basically an entrepreneur of the candy stick trade anyway, you can spare two bottles."

story:
Matthew slotted into the lobby just as the clan banner flashed up: "Scavengers, Room 4, 7 p.m. sharp." He dreaded these evenings lately, because someone kept typing things in the public chat that made the whole room go quiet. Not swearing, exactly. Just sharp little jabs, aimed at whoever played worst that night. Last week it was Francesco, who had logged off without a word.

Tonight the lobby was almost full. Jaelynn's mic crackled first. "Matthew, check the clan chat before we queue." Her voice was low, like she didn't want the room to hear, even though everyone could. He flipped to the private channel. There it was again, from the username ShadowVex: "Some people here don't deserve a spot on the roster." No name attached. That was the trick of it, Matthew thought. In the public chat ShadowVex was all thumbs-up and "nice pull," but in the private channel the tone turned like a coin.

He didn't reply right away. Instead he typed a message everyone could see: "Anyone know if there's like, official rules for how to act online? For real, written down somewhere?" ShadowVex answered fast. "Lol it's a game, not a library."

But Jaelynn didn't laugh. "Actually," she typed slowly, "my cousin did a project on this." She read out loud through the mic: "One of the first written guides to online manners was published in 1995, called 'Netiquette Guidelines.' It was a document called RFC 1855."

"RFC what now?" Francesco said, popping into the voice channel at last.

"Netiquette Guidelines," Matthew repeated, writing it down. He was already hatching a test. If he posted the rules in the public chat where everyone watched, ShadowVex would have to act nice. But if the rules only went to the private channel, the jabs would keep coming, because the room wouldn't know they existed. Tone changed depending on who was watching. That was the pattern he wanted to prove.

He typed the rules into the public lobby chat, one line at a time, keeping the wording consistent with what Jaelynn had read. "No calling out players by name. Public and private chat, same standard. Signed, RFC 1855, 1995." The room paused. Then someone sent a slow clap emoji. Then another. ShadowVex typed "okok calm down" and, for the first time all week, nothing sharp followed.

The twist came at match end, when Francesco unmuted with a strange cough. "So, um. ShadowVex is my little brother. He was using my second account." Dead silence. "He said the roster spot thing because he's scared I'll get cut and stop playing with him. I didn't know how to say it in front of everyone."

Matthew stared at the chat box for a long second. Then he typed, "Bring him to Room 4 tomorrow. Everyone starts somewhere."

Jaelynn's mic crackled. "That," she said, "is an adaptation even RFC 1855 didn't cover."

story:
The after-school light through the library's tall windows turned the dust above the tables luminous, and Katherine squinted at her photocopy of the scene between Macbeth and Lady Macbeth until the letters blurred. Ms. Yip had assigned each group four speeches to paraphrase into modern English, and Katherine's group had exactly one afternoon and two members, since Bryan had a dentist appointment.

"You go first," Rio said, sliding the paper toward her. "You're better at old words than me."

Katherine read the second line aloud. " 'He that's coming must be provided for.' That one's easy. Somebody who is coming has to be dealt with." She underlined it. Then she hit the next speech and stopped. " 'All hail, Macbeth, that shalt be king hereafter.' Shalt. Is that shall, or should?"

"Should," Rio said, with visible skepticism. "Like, you should be king someday."

Katherine didn't answer right away. She ran her finger down the page, hunting for a pattern the way she hunted for the rule in a math problem, something consistent underneath the strange spellings. She counted. "Look. Doth. Hath. Speaks not. Thou shalt. Every single time there's a weird ending, it's on the he or she verb. Not on the I or you verbs."

"So?"

"So it's like the endings are attached to who's doing the action. Watch." She pulled a second sheet from her binder, a page from Romeo and Juliet Ms. Yip had handed out as extra practice, and scanned it. "Here. 'She hath.' And here, 'he doth.' Same endings, same kind of subject. And hath must mean has. Like he who hath gold. It's in songs and stuff." She wrote in the margin of the Macbeth sheet: doth means does, hath means has. Then she tested it against a line she already understood. " 'It hath the primal eldest curse upon it.' It has the curse. That works. That actually works."

Rio leaned over. "Then shalt isn't should. Shalt is shall. 'You shall be king hereafter.' Not maybe. Definitely."

They went through the whole scene with the rule, and the speeches stopped being fog and started being arguments between two people, one ambitious and one frightened. Katherine tried to quantify their progress, ticking each paraphrased line with her pencil, and got to fourteen out of eighteen before the library lights flicked, which meant Ms. Yip was closing up.

At the circulation desk, Ms. Yip glanced at Katherine's margins. "Nice notes. You cracked the endings?"

"Tested it on two different plays," Katherine said. "Same pattern both times."

Ms. Yip stamped Rio's book and slid it across the counter. "Then you're ready for the harder question. Who's more afraid in that scene, him or her?"

The tomato plants in Mr. He's garden had lost eleven tomatoes in three nights, and Cole wanted to find out what was taking them. He never saw anything. The fruits were there at dusk and gone by morning, with no tracks and no dropped bits anywhere. Eleanor came over with her notebook and stood at the fence beside him in the humid evening air.

"Okay, so we have a guess," she said. "Rats. But we can't see them, so we have to test it." They negotiated for a while over how to do it. Cole wanted to wrap two plants in netting and leave two plants bare. Eleanor wanted to coat two plants in hot pepper spray and leave the rest alone. In the end, being in a hurry, they did both at once: netting and pepper on the same two plants, nothing on the others.

The next morning the bare plants had lost four more tomatoes and the protected ones had lost none. "It worked," Cole said, and Eleanor wrote it down. But then she stopped, pen in the air. "Wait. We changed two things. Netting and pepper. So we don't know which one did it. Maybe the rats hate the pepper. Maybe they can't get through the netting. Maybe either one alone would work."

Cole sat on the fence rail and thought about that. His father had once tried to fix a slow garage door by replacing the spring and oiling the track on the same day, and afterwards he couldn't say which repair had mattered. It was the same problem here. "So tomorrow we split it up," he said. "One plant with netting only, one with pepper only, one with nothing." Eleanor nodded and drew a chart with three columns. "My brother calls that the independent variable," she said. "It's the one thing you change on purpose to see what happens." Cole copied the phrase into his own notebook, under a heading that said WHICH ONE.

They set it up that evening. The next morning there was dew on the netting and a rabbit at the far fence, sitting still, watching them. Cole looked at the pepper-only plant, where two tomatoes were gone, and at the netting-only plant, where every tomato hung untouched. He turned to Eleanor and pointed at the rabbit. "New guess."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
story:
Charlie spread the two graphs across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with salt shakers. One showed a city called Iquitos, with rainfall bars that climbed every month like a staircase to nowhere. The other showed Cairo, where the bars lay flat against the bottom of the page. Ms. Petrov had promised the class would have to defend their answers tomorrow, and Charlie hated being the one who guessed.

Her laptop chimed. Isra's face filled the screen, her own graphs half visible behind her. "Did you finish classifying?"

"No," Charlie said. "I keep switching my answer for Iquitos."

"Then you're violating your own rule," Isra said. "You told us yesterday, stop guessing and use the system."

Charlie pulled up the page in her textbook. The Koppen system, it said, sorted climates by numbers, not by how a place looked. For a tropical rainforest climate, the rule ran down the page like a checklist: every month of the year had to average at least 18 degrees Celsius, and every month had to get at least 60 millimeters of rain. Every single month. No exceptions allowed.

She grabbed a pencil and started at January on the Iquitos graph. Temperature first. January sat at 26 degrees. She drew a light line at 18 across the whole year, like a fence, and checked each month against it. February cleared the fence. March cleared it. She worked through the year month by month, and none of the temperature curves dipped below her line.

"Now the rain," she muttered. She set her ruler at 60 millimeters on the rainfall axis and drew a second fence. This one was harder. January's bar towered past 200. April's bar barely cleared 60, but it cleared it. June, July, August, each one stood above the line. December wavered at what looked like exactly 60, and she squinted, leaned closer, and checked the number printed at the top of the bar. 62. Still above.

"It passes," she said to Isra. "All twelve months pass both tests. Iquitos counts as a tropical rainforest under Koppen."

"Try Cairo," Isra said. "For contrast."

Charlie laid her fences on the Cairo graph. The temperature line dove below 18 in three winter months, and the rainfall bars never once reached 60. Two failures, over and over. Same planet, she thought, same spinning ball of water and air, and one place grew lush green forest while the other grew sand. The graph was the only evidence she had, and it was enough. Somewhere behind those bars was the reason, invisible, but the numbers didn't lie about what it produced.

Her brother thumped past with a box of model airplane cargo, scattering small plastic crates across the table edge. Charlie swept them off her graphs and pinned the last corner down with her coffee mug.

"So tomorrow when Ms. Petrov asks," Isra said, "you'll actually have a method?"

Charlie capped her pencil and smiled at the two graphs, fences still drawn across them. "Every month, both lines. That's my whole defense."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Anna had been to the cultural center for craft fairs and a lunar new year show, but never for this. The hallway smelled of cardamom and butter, and Thomas was already waiting by the doors, bouncing on his heels like the floor was hot.

"You came," he said. "Good. My cousins will outnumber you, but you'll survive."

Inside, the big hall was full of tables, and Anna noticed something odd right away. There were plates stacked everywhere, samosas and dates and some kind of sweet noodles, but nobody was eating. Kids were laughing, aunties were hugging, a man in a bright green robe was arranging a tray of pastries like a general deploying troops. All that food, and not one bite taken. It was a mystery, and Anna loved mysteries more than she loved homework, which is to say a lot.

She watched Thomas's little cousin grab a date, lift it halfway to his mouth, then sigh and put it back. Anna leaned toward Thomas. "Is the food broken? Poisoned? Some kind of decorative food?"

"It's Eid al-Fitr," Thomas said. "That means it's the end of Ramadan, the month where the grown-ups fast. No food from dawn until sunset. A whole month."

Anna did the math slowly, the way she did with riddles. A month of not eating all day. That would explain the tower of pastries, the cousin's dramatic sigh, the man guarding the tray like a dragon. But she wanted proof. "So nobody has eaten since sunrise?" she whispered. "Even the little kids?"

"Some do, some don't," Thomas said. "But my grandmother, never. She says her streak is cumulative. Thirty years of Ramadans, all stacked up."

Then the man in the green robe cupped his hands, the room went quiet, and a voice called out across the hall. The sun had gone down. Anna watched the whole crowd move at once, like one enormous hungry organism with forty arms, and the pastry tray simply vanished, flourishing into nothing while the man in green blinked at his empty hands.

The little cousin ate his date, then five more, then announced to the room, "I have waited my whole life for this," which was three hours, but nobody argued. Thomas's grandmother pressed a pastry into Anna's palm, warm and sticky, and said, "Eat, eat, you are too skinny for a detective."

Anna froze. "How did you know I was investigating?"

"Child, you have been staring at that tray since you walked in." She laughed and patted Anna's cheek. "Next mystery, I suggest the sweet noodles. They vanish fast."

Anna bit into the pastry and turned to Thomas. "So next year, I'm bringing my own plate. And a seat near the front."

Thomas grinned. "Bring a helmet too," he said, and pointed at the empty table where the samosas used to be.

The click started three nights ago, somewhere inside the garage door opener, and it was getting louder. Gabrielle sat on an overturned milk crate in her family's garage workshop, her dad's old workbench behind her, and listened. Click, pause, click. The door went up and down fine, which was the strange part. Something hidden was making the noise, and she wanted to know what.

Elio arrived first, skateboarding up the driveway, then Malek on his bike. They crowded around the opener's metal case while Gabrielle found a screwdriver in the drawer of bolts and drill bits. "It could be the motor," Elio said. "Or a loose screw rattling around." Malek crouched and put his ear against the case. "Do it again," he said, and Gabrielle pressed the button on the wall. The door rumbled upward. Click, pause, click.

"It clicks twice each time, always in the same rhythm," Malek said. "Loose screws don't keep a rhythm." Gabrielle turned the screwdriver and lifted the cover off. Inside she could see the motor, the gears, and a diagonal metal arm that swung as the door moved. She watched it go around, and around, and then she saw it: a small plastic gear with a chip taken out of one tooth. Each time the chipped tooth met the next gear, it slipped, and clicked. "There," she said, pointing. "The gear's broken."

Elio leaned in, frowning. "So how do we know that's really it? We can't watch it every second." Gabrielle thought of the poster she'd made last month for the science fair, the one where she'd written about how plants might respond to sound, and how Mr. Demetriou had looked at it and asked, "How would you test that?" She hadn't been able to answer then, but she'd gone home and figured it out afterward. "You write it as an if-then statement," she said. "Hypotheses are often written as 'If ..., then ...' statements, which name the change being made and the result that is predicted." She picked up a pencil stub and wrote on the back of a sandpaper sheet: If we stop the gear from slipping, then the clicking stops.

"Okay," Malek said slowly. "So what's the change?"

"A little tape won't hold," Gabrielle said, "but if the chipped tooth can't catch on anything, it can't slip." She pressed a small dab of grease onto the broken tooth with a cotton swab, then wiped the swab clean. Elio watched the gears hungrily, as if they might consume the grease and fail anyway. The gear itself was made of a cheap polymer, some kind of soft plastic, which was probably why the tooth had broken in the first place.

Gabrielle pressed the button. The door rumbled down. Silence. She pressed it again, and the door went up through the same quiet, no click, no pause, nothing. Malek pumped his fist. From the driveway, Mr. Demetriou, who had been washing his car across the street, called over, "You three fixed that yourselves?" Gabrielle held up the sandpaper with the if-then sentence on it and grinned. "Tested it," she said. "And the test said we were right."

story:
Felix had exactly forty minutes before boarding, and the climate project was due the moment he landed. He spread his papers across three plastic seats at Gate 14, next to the window where the tarmac shimmered with heat. His bag held two graphs, one for the Atacama Desert and one for a rainforest in Brazil, and a half-finished paragraph comparing them. His phone buzzed.

"Did you finish the analysis?" Alisa texted. "Mr. Greco said he'd fail anyone who just describes the graphs."

Felix typed back, "Working on it now. Airport wifi is terrible." He laid the Atacama graph flat. For the rainforest, every month had a tall bar showing rainfall, some nearly three hundred millimeters, and the temperature line stayed warm and steady all year. The desert graph was strange. A few months had short bars, barely slivers, but most months had nothing at all. No bar, not even a tiny one. He'd assumed he'd copied it wrong.

He called Malaika, who was on the trip with him, waiting in line for pretzels. "My desert graph is broken," he said. "Half the months don't have rainfall bars. I must have missed them when I redrew it."

"Wait," Malaika said, chewing. "I read the same thing when I made my graph. Some of those weather stations in the Atacama have never recorded rain. Not a drop. So the missing bars are real. That's not a mistake, that's the whole point."

Felix stared at the graph while a suitcase rattled past and a speaker crackled overhead about a delay in Miami. If the missing bars were real, then the comparison wasn't tall bars versus short bars. It was bars versus empty space. That empty space implied something stronger than any number he could write down. He flipped his notebook to a fresh page. The paragraph could hinge on that one fact: a place where the rain gauge has never once caught rain, set beside a forest that measures its rain in hundreds of millimeters every month.

"But is it credible?" he asked Malaika. "No rain ever? That sounds like a rumor someone made up for a project."

"Look it up yourself," she said. "I have to get my pretzel."

He searched on the airport wifi, which took three tries and one restart, and there it was: parts of Chile's Atacama Desert were so dry that some weather stations there had never recorded rain. He read the sentence twice, then carefully copied the graph's empty months into his paragraph, explaining that the blank spaces were data, not gaps. The announcer called early boarding for families, and a woman with a stroller wheeled past his seat.

When Mr. Greco walked by on his way to the same flight, his lanyard swinging, Felix waved him over. "Mr. Greco, my desert graph has months with no bars at all. Can blank space count as data?" Mr. Greco leaned down, read two lines, and tapped the empty columns with one finger.

"That's the best thing on the page," he said. "Don't touch it."

Felix wrote his final sentence as the gate agent called his row, zipped his bag, and ran for the jet bridge with the graph still warm from his hands.
